items.explanation: The 1639 fine — levied with no statute authorizing it — is cited as evidence that Massachusetts Bay still operated a moral economy of 'just price' and 'just wage' rather than unrestrained individualism: communal fairness norms overrode even the absence of written law.
options: (A) Poor New Englanders were using the courts mainly to vent class resentment against wealthy merchants.
(B) Bribery and favoritism routinely corrupted legal proceedings in Puritan New England.
(C) Puritan magistrates punished rich and poor alike for expressing unorthodox religious opinions.
(D) Puritan leaders imposed a moral economy of communal fairness over free-market individualism.
items.stem: In the second paragraph, the authors bring up the 1639 case of a wealthy merchant fined for excessive profit chiefly to illustrate which point?
items.stimulus: Although some Puritan values resembled the rising capitalist ethic, Puritan economic life remained closer to the medieval than the modern. Unrestrained economic individualism would have alarmed any respectable Puritan. The statute books and court records of seventeenth-century Massachusetts are full of government-set price and wage controls. Puritans treated wealth as a trust from God, stressing duties and responsibilities alongside the benefits of work and gain. In 1639 the colony's General Court fined one of its richest merchants for excessive profiteering — though no statute prohibited the practice. The Puritans never separated religion from business and kept repeating the medieval idea of the 'just price.' Over the long run, though, once the Puritan work ethic was divorced from its religious setting, it quickened the spirit of capitalism: the old restraints on the individual gradually gave way to the enterprising, self-made figure who rose by his own exertions. — adapted from Gerald N. Grob and Robert N. Beck, American Ideas (1963)

items.explanation: The passage's thesis is the paradox: Puritan asceticism and the 'calling' bred hard work and wealth, and as strict religious orthodoxy faded, those work habits fused with market freedom — producing a market-oriented economy out of a moral one.
options: (A) Puritan limits on trade kept New England's economy permanently behind the southern and middle colonies.
(B) New England under the Puritans reproduced the feudal manor system of medieval Europe, with estates passing from father to son over generations.
(C) As Puritan orthodoxy faded, Puritan work habits fused with freer markets into a market economy.
(D) New England's economy began to grow only after non-Puritan immigrants arrived in large numbers after 1640.
items.stem: Which statement best captures the main argument the authors make in the passage?

items.explanation: Josephe describes beatings, theft of goods, and unpaid forced labor as the rebels' motives — a direct response to Spanish colonial exploitation (encomienda/repartimiento labor, tribute, suppression of religion), culminating in the coordinated 1680 uprising led by Popé.
options: (A) The willing adoption of Spanish cultural and religious practices by Pueblo peoples.
(B) Organized resistance by Pueblo peoples to Spanish colonial exploitation and coercion.
(C) Widespread intermarriage blending Spanish and Pueblo communities into a single society.
(D) Warfare between rival Pueblo groups triggered by Spanish forced relocation policies.
items.stem: The events Josephe describes in his testimony best exemplify which of the following?
items.stimulus: Asked what drove the rebels to renounce Spanish authority, Josephe — a Spanish-speaking Pueblo Indian questioned by colonial officials after the 1680 uprising — answered that the causes were the ill treatment they suffered: Spanish officials beat them, seized their property, and forced them to work without pay. Asked why the rebels burned churches and images, mocked sacred objects, and killed priests, Josephe said he had heard it stated that while besieging the Spanish villa the rebels shouted that the Spaniards' God was dead and that only their own gods lived. Their captains ordered that the names of Jesus and Mary never be spoken, and Josephe reported seeing new houses of native worship built where the people danced their traditional ceremonial dances. — paraphrased from the 1681 interrogation of Josephe

items.explanation: The rebels burned churches, banned the names of Jesus and Mary, and rebuilt native ceremonial houses — attacking the religious-cultural apparatus of colonization alongside the labor/tribute system, i.e., a bid for cultural and political autonomy, not just economic redress.
options: (A) The rebels had been so thoroughly Christianized that their uprising was purely an economic protest.
(B) The rebels limited themselves to peaceful, nonviolent forms of protest against Spanish rule.
(C) The rebels attacked Spanish religious and cultural symbols as well as the colonial labor system.
(D) The rebels traded freely with the Spanish and rebelled only against new taxes on that trade.
items.stem: Josephe's testimony indicates that the Pueblo rebels did which of the following?

items.explanation: After retaking New Mexico in the 1690s, Spanish authorities shifted policy: they appointed an official to defend Pueblo rights, tolerated some native religious practices, and relied more on missionary persuasion — a limited accommodation, distinct from the Anglo pattern of removal.
options: (A) Spanish authorities accommodated certain aspects of Pueblo culture in the late 1600s and 1700s.
(B) Spanish armies and disease completely eliminated the Pueblo population of the Southwest.
(C) Defeated by the rebels, Spain permanently abandoned all its territorial claims in North America by 1700.
(D) Spain and Britain allied to impose joint European control over the interior of North America.
items.stem: Which of the following best describes Spanish policy in the region in the decades after the events Josephe describes?
